text: 13:40. Thirty percent of mobile logins are failing. Seven services are red. Three deploys, a config change and a feature flag landed in the last hour. So... which one broke production?

Meet Hypocenter. Built for Graph Hacks by Raghav Gupta, a student, on FalkorDB. It's an on-call agent that follows the alerts down to where an outage started, and proves the fix before anyone approves it.

It lives by one rule: no path, no blame. A change is a suspect only if the graph connects it to the symptom, and the alerts climb that path in order. The epicenter is where you feel it. The hypocenter is where it started.

Everything lives in one graph per company: services and who calls whom, owners and the on-call rota, deploys, pods, the team's chat, and every incident it has already solved. Click the cube, and it comes apart into its node types.

Let's start with a real failure, from the public RCAEval benchmark: a CPU fault inside Online Boutique. Six services alert. Nothing was deployed. Hypocenter finds currencyservice failed first, and the alerts climbed back up in order. Infrastructure. Page its owners. That's exactly the benchmark's answer.

Now, back to 13:40. Four agents take the incident: triage, investigator, skeptic, responder. They never talk to each other in code. Each one writes its handoff into the graph, and the next one reads it back. Live, every step with its Cypher.

The verdict: the auth deploy, at 13:34. Auth alerted at 13:38, mobile at 13:40. In order. A flag on users sits on the same path, but users never alerted, so it's out. And the other alerts? Three separate problems, two of them belonging to other incidents.
Then comes the evidence gate. Eight named checks, each with the exact query that decided it. All eight pass: confirmed. Cut the path, and it doesn't guess. It says: the graph can't prove this.

The agent can only propose. Before you approve, the fix runs on a copy of the graph. It clears auth and mobile, and leaves everything else alone. Approve it, and Hypocenter checks the alerts really cleared.
Replay plays the whole investigation back, lighting up each service the moment it's reached.
Break it lets you change the graph and watch the verdict move. Cut auth out of the call path, and the deploy gives way. Every experiment runs on a copy that's thrown away.

The organisers asked for one test: the same question, at depth one and at depth four. At one hop, it blames a victim, with high confidence. From two hops down, it finds the real pool change. And ask about a service that doesn't exist? Not modelled. Not safe.
It knows the company, too. Ask why that pool change was made, and the answer comes straight from the team's chat. Then ask who owns it, and it remembers what it means.
And before the next deploy, Ship it says ship, review, or hold, with every reason from the graph.

So, does it actually work? All 360 real RCAEval failures, against the benchmark's own baselines: the right service first, 81 percent of the time. On ninety held-out failures, NSigma beats it, 76 to 71. And the README says so. Zero wrong high-confidence calls.
Each of the eight FalkorDB algorithms has a test that changes what it reads, and watches the decision flip. Pull FalkorDB out, and there's no answer at all.
242 tests. 28 deliberate breakages, all caught. Live on the web, and one command to run it yourself. This is Hypocenter, built by Raghav Gupta. No path, no blame.
